title: Tbh, how much sleep I got the night before affects my theatre reviews...
transcript: There are definitely factors outside of the show itself that are going to affect my review of the show. But when I think of that list, how much I spend on the ticket personally is at the bottom of that list. And that's not to say that it doesn't affect my review at all. But when I'm reviewing a show, I am thinking of what I'm seeing on the stage in terms of design, of storytelling, of what they're trying to do. And if anything, the cost of the ticket is going to affect my emotion towards that, but not the actual criticism of the show. For example, last year I saw Othello for $20. I did not get invited to the show. It just happened to be right place, right time, where I was about ready to go see HadesTown, two blocks away, and somebody listed their ticket for sale for $20 because they couldn't make the show time, like 20 minutes before curtain. And so I pivoted real fast to go see Othello because I knew it was the only chance I was going to get, given that I have a budget of under $100. And I truly hated that production. Like, it was not for me. I thought the celebrities were miscast and misdirected. I thought the design was lacking. And that was not at all affected by the fact that I got a 20 dollar ticket. What was affected by the fact that I got a 20 dollar ticket is. I think I would have been exponentially even more mad had I paid full price for that show. Right. Like, my criticisms would have stayed the same, the emotion definitely would have gone up. To be honest, I spend so much money on theatre, I, I mean, I do a theatre wrapped every year where I show you the thousands of dollars that I'm still spending on tickets, despite even still getting invites to a good chunk of shows. So for me personally, dropping up to $100 on a show is out of sight, out of mind. I'm not thinking about that when I'm reviewing a show. What is going to affect my review more than anything is where I'm sitting in the theatre. And that does get affected on whether or not I'm purchasing my own tickets. But to be honest, the way that I get the best seats in a theatre is not going as an influencer through the marketing team, it's going as a critic through the press team. Because professional theatre critics are given the best seats in the house. If it's a general admission theatre, they are often given reserved seats so they don't have to get there as early. They are getting prime orchestra seats. When we're given free tickets as influencers, that's not always a guarantee. We often have partial view seats. I've seen maybe happy ending seven times and the two worst seats I've ever Gotten were when I was invited by the show, they just put me in the partial view seats. Professional theatre critics who were brought in by the press team to go review that show were given centre orchestra tickets. And professional theatre critics, mind you, are paid for their reviews. Not necessarily a ton. Some publications do not pay their people a lot, but those critics are usually getting paid, and those theatre critics are also seeing the show for free. I find it frustrating when we put all of this criticism on content creators, because theatre critics are often given the same privileges, if not even more privileges, than content creators, and yet we often view them as this completely impartial third party because they're hired by a publication. And it gets especially frustrating when there's content creators like myself who consider ourselves theatre critics and yet we are not treated as such because we exist on a social media platform. But I feel like that's. That's a. A larger conversation, right? At the end of the day, just because I'm getting a free ticket to a show does not mean that I feel obligated to give that show a good review. In the same way that the critic for the New York Times doesn't give everything a Critics Pick just because they got a free ticket to go review that show.
